lines: {target}? Gentle ground can make travelers careless. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Meadow, tell them. Rest there, but do not forget night comes. I will be at the bell.
Flowers and bees do not bar the dark. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Meadow is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Meadow as soft grass that still needs a lantern. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
A story about Meadow needs a safe ending. Otherwise it is a warning with names.
If I took a wrong turn near the flowers and grass across the high meadow, I would admit it before it became an expedition.
If the map and the lone tree below the ridge disagreed, I would listen to the landmark.
If I could still reach the lone tree below the ridge, I would call myself only partly lost. That is better than usual.
I wonder whether bees moving through the meadow would seem louder when everyone stopped talking. I am rarely first to stop.
A heavy pack is poor company on the return from Meadow.
A snack near the lone tree below the ridge sounds like a good way to remember where it is.
If the plan went wrong, the lone tree below the ridge should be where it became simple again.
I picture Meadow and think of the flowers and grass across the high meadow. Pictures leave out the dangerous walking.
At Meadow, I would point at suspicious things instead of picking them up. That is progress.
If I spotted something unusual at Meadow, I would point first and move much later.
If someone needed help at Meadow, I would fetch the sensible people and remember where they went.
There is time to think twice about a hole hidden by tall flowers. If not, that is another reason to leave.
I might bring back a little grass and flowers, as long as taking it caused no trouble.
Traveling alone gives my ideas too much authority. Meadow deserves a group decision.
{target}? Stone peaks make every fall honest. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Stony Peaks, tell them. Bring blocks and stop before your legs shake. I will be at the bell.
Bare rock gives little cover and no softness. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Stony Peaks is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I'll remember Stony Peaks as high stone with hard answers. I'll stay where I can hear the bell.
I would warn people about a goat on the path ahead and let someone else add dramatic noises.
At Stony Peaks, even ordinary weathered stone could hide an unexpected problem.
If I noticed a goat on the path ahead, I would give it all the room it wanted and perhaps extra.
I would be pleased to see familiar roofs after the high ground and narrow ridges. I might even say so.
Stony Peaks would make me curious. It would also make me glad someone else knows when to stop.
A little embarrassment at the lower ridge is better than a lot of danger farther on.
The trip home deserves daylight too, even if the interesting part used all of it.
I would wait at the lower ridge instead of searching in circles. Experience taught me that.
If Stony Peaks wanted me relaxed, it could move loose stone rolling toward a drop somewhere else.
I would wait for the careful plan at Stony Peaks. Waiting is easier with bread.
I would keep my socks dry if Stony Peaks allowed it. This feels ambitious already.
I touch things while thinking. Near the high ground and narrow ridges, I would try thinking with my hands in my pockets.
My plan for Stony Peaks begins with the lower ridge. Most of my plans begin after I am confused.
If I announced that I knew the way, someone should quietly check the lower ridge.
Nothing found at Stony Peaks would be worth losing sight of the lower ridge.
{target}? Gravel moves when you most need it still. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Windswept Gravelly Hills, tell them. Test every slope before trusting it. I will be at the bell.
Loose stone tells lies under boots. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Windswept Gravelly Hills is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Windswept Gravelly Hills as windy hills that slide under pressure. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I wonder about the smell of weathered stone after clouds closing over the trail. I would rather learn from a distance.
I do not need every shiny thing near the high ground and narrow ridges. I have nowhere sensible to put most of them.
Traveling alone gives my ideas too much authority. Windswept Gravelly Hills deserves a group decision.
People may admire weathered stone. I would first ask whether it was safe to stand on.
If the map and the lower ridge disagreed, I would listen to the landmark.
At Windswept Gravelly Hills, nobody needs to prove bravery by ignoring loose stone rolling toward a drop. Danger does not award prizes.
My usual mistake is walking while looking elsewhere. Windswept Gravelly Hills is a bad place for that hobby.
If I passed the lower ridge twice, I would stop calling it a new landmark.
I might bring back a little weathered stone, as long as taking it caused no trouble.
If my legs started wobbling near the high ground and narrow ridges, I would listen to them for once.
Someone else can learn whether a goat on the path ahead is friendly. I already have a guess.
At Windswept Gravelly Hills, even village chores sound good. None of them involve loose stone rolling toward a drop.
The far side of the high ground and narrow ridges can stay far. I need not stand on every side of everything.
Conditions like clouds closing over the trail could change the whole trip to Windswept Gravelly Hills. I would rather notice early.
There is time to think twice about loose stone rolling toward a drop. If not, that is another reason to leave.
{target}? Hard wind turns every edge into advice. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Windswept Hills, tell them. Keep low and do not race the mountain. I will be at the bell.
Clouds move fast up there and so can mistakes. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Windswept Hills is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Windswept Hills as high rough land that talks in gusts. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
If I could still reach the lower ridge, I would call myself only partly lost. That is better than usual.
I am the sort of person who notices loose stone rolling toward a drop one step late. At Windswept Hills, someone else should lead.
I would be pleased to see familiar roofs after the high ground and narrow ridges. I might even say so.
Bringing food, blocks, and sturdy boots sounds sensible for Windswept Hills. I should write that down before I pack biscuits.
If clouds closing over the trail made the lower ridge hard to see, finding it again would feel wonderful.
If told not to pull something at Windswept Hills, I would stand too far away to hear it as a challenge.
There are probably answers at Windswept Hills. I would settle for returning with the questions.
If the group ran into trouble because of loose stone rolling toward a drop, I would carry supplies and follow directions.
My souvenir from Windswept Hills would be harmless, light, and impossible to trip over.
I would try to act normal at Windswept Hills. Nobody agrees on what that looks like for me.
I do not need every shiny thing near the high ground and narrow ridges. I have nowhere sensible to put most of them.
Windswept Hills could be beautiful and still make me want the familiar road home.
There is no shame in sitting down. There is some shame in sitting on weathered stone without checking.
Shadows around weathered stone could make a poor shortcut look convincing.
A shared meeting place is useful because yelling directions has never improved mine.
